To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Japanese EM1 industry's rise was the result of the translation of digital sound synthesis technology from the US semiconductor industry, that this process of technology transfer was a complex one that involved a number of different actors, and that the Japanese firms that were most successful in this process were those that were able to translate this new technology in ways that enabled them to overcome the limitations of the new technology.

the transition from analog to digital sound synthesis, a transectorial innovation that occurred in the 1980s and early 1990s, led to a spatial discontinuity in which Japanese firms in Hamamatsu replaced the US as the world's leading producers of electronic musical instruments, and; that this spatial discontinuity was facilitated by the translation of codified knowledge from the US to Hamamatsu, a process that involved the redefinition of technological boundaries and a reconfiguration of the industry's knowledge

the rise of Hamamatsu as an industrial cluster in the EMI industry was due to the successful transfer of digital technology from the US to Hamamatsu and that this technology transfer, in turn, was due to the ability of Japanese engineers to translate digital technology into analog technology

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the thesis demonstrates how a transectorial technological discontinuity, in this case digital to analog sound synthesizer technology, can be the trigger for a spatial shift in an industrial cluster.

the case study of the EMI industry shows that the translation of knowledge is an important but often underappreciated aspect of the geography of innovation, especially during episodes of radical change when transectorial innovation plays a key role in shaping the industrial landscape.
the Japanese EM1 industry's rise and fall was the outcome of a series of interrelated technological and institutional changes that were both endogenous to the industry and exogenous to it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the study of transectorial innovation can be a powerful tool for understanding the social and geographical dimensions of inter sectoral technological change.
we have tried to understand how a new technological paradigm, the digital revolution, affected the geography of an old technological paradigm, the analog revolution.

this thesis contributes to the literature on innovation and regional development by highlighting the importance of codification and translation for knowledge formation in the face of radical technological change.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the social and institutional context of innovation is crucial to understanding the geography of innovation.
the translation of codified knowledge from one sector to another is a critical but neglected dimension of innovation and industrial change.
the translation of codified knowledge is a critical component of the process of intersectoral innovation and that it is a key factor in the emergence of regional industrial clusters.
